title: Does lightning never strike the same place twice?
hook: Christ the Redeemer would beg to differ.
summary: It does: lightning often hits tall, isolated objects again and again, and Christ the Redeemer is struck several times a year.

cardBlocks.text: The saying goes that lightning never strikes the same place twice. Science says otherwise: lightning often strikes the same spot repeatedly, especially if it is tall, pointy and isolated. Height, a pointed shape and isolation are the main factors deciding where a bolt will land.

The proof is in Rio de Janeiro. The Christ the Redeemer statue, on top of Corcovado mountain, is hit by lightning several times a year: estimates from INPE, Brazil’s space research institute, range from three to five to about six a year. Some strikes have damaged the statue, such as those that hit the fingers of its right hand.
Lightning strikes the same place many times, above all tall, isolated spots like Christ the Redeemer.

deepDiveBlocks.text: In the United States, the Empire State Building is hit an average of 23 times a year, according to the country’s National Weather Service.
Metal makes no difference to where lightning strikes. Trees and mountains, tall and isolated but with little or no metal, also get struck many times a year.
